t: Seventeenth Amendment: Popular election of senators
x: Before 1913, state legislatures picked U.S. senators. The Seventeenth Amendment gave that choice to the voters. Anyone who can vote for the state Assembly can vote for Senate, and a governor can fill a vacancy temporarily if state law allows it. California law allows it, and Williams handles a vacant council seat with a similar appoint-or-elect choice. Key takeaways Passed by Congress May 13, 1912; ratified April 8, 1913. It modified Article I, §3 . Senators are "elected by the people thereof," two per state, for six years . The people who can vote for Senate are the people who can vote for the "most numerous branch" of the state legislature . In California, that's the Assembly. A governor can make a temporary appointment until an election, but only if the legislature allows it. California's does . In Williams: when a council seat opens, the council must appoint someone or call a special election within 60 days .

t: Seventeenth Amendment: Popular election of senators
x: Official text Amendment XVII read in context : Amendment XVII The Senate of the United States shall be composed of two Senators from each State, elected by the people thereof, for six years; and each Senator shall have one vote. The electors in each State shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. When vacancies happen in the representation of any State in the Senate, the executive authority of such State shall issue writs of election to fill such vacancies: Provided, That the legislature of any State may empower the executive thereof to make temporary appointments until the people fill the vacancies by election as the legislature may direct. This amendment shall not be so construed as to affect the election or term of any Senator chosen before it becomes valid as part of the Constitution. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Seventeenth Amendment: Popular election of senators
x: "Two Senators from each State, elected by the people thereof, for six years." Equal representation per state and six-year terms are unchanged from the original Constitution. Only the electors changed . Who votes. "The electors in each State shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures" . California's own rule is short: "A United States citizen 18 years of age and resident in this State may vote" (Art. II, §2) . Vacancies. The governor must "issue writs of election to fill such vacancies," but "the legislature of any State may empower the executive thereof to make temporary appointments until the people fill the vacancies by election as the legislature may direct" . No effect on sitting senators. The amendment did not cut short the term of anyone chosen before it took effect .

t: Seventeenth Amendment: Popular election of senators
x: Under Article I, §3, senators were "chosen by the Legislature thereof" . By the early 1900s, critics pointed to "deadlocks within legislatures resulting in vacancies remaining unfilled for substantial intervals" and to "the influencing of legislative selection by corrupt political organizations and special interest groups through purchase of legislative seats" . States worked around the system before it formally changed. They set up primaries so voters could "designate their preference for one of several party candidates for a senatorial seat and state legislatures generally elected the winning candidate" . By 1912, "at least twenty-nine states were nominating Senators on a popular basis," so legislatures had little more discretion than "that retained by presidential electors" . The amendment made popular election mandatory everywhere.

t: Seventeenth Amendment: Popular election of senators
x: Race and Senate primaries. A federal appeals court held that Georgia party officials who barred a Black citizen from a Senate primary violated the Seventeenth Amendment ( Chapman v. King , 1946; the Supreme Court declined review) . No extra qualifications. States can't add their own qualifications for Congress, such as term limits. In the Court's words, a state-by-state "patchwork" would be "inconsistent with the Framers' vision of a uniform National Legislature representing the people of the United States" ( U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton , 514 U.S. 779 (1995)) . Equal districts. Wesberry v. Sanders applied one person, one vote to U.S. House districts ( Wesberry v. Sanders , 376 U.S. 1 (1964)) . Senate seats are statewide, so every California voter's Senate vote counts the same.

t: Seventeenth Amendment: Popular election of senators
x: Voting for Senate. Williams voters elect California's senators in statewide elections run locally by the Colusa County elections office . If a Senate seat opens. The Governor "may appoint and commission an elector of this state who possesses the qualifications for the office to temporarily fill the vacancy until a person is elected at a statewide general election" (Elections Code §10720) . If a council seat opens. The City Council faces the same appoint-or-elect choice. It "shall, within 60 days from the commencement of the vacancy, either fill the vacancy by appointment or call a special election to fill the vacancy" (Gov. Code §36512) . An appointee usually serves only until the next general municipal election, depending on timing . Our reading: at both levels the law accepts a short-term appointment to keep the seat filled, then sends the choice back to voters. If a council vacancy comes up, the agenda item and public comment are your chance to weigh in. See how to comment .

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: The Eighteenth Amendment banned making, selling and transporting "intoxicating liquors" across the country. Prohibition began in January 1920 and ended in 1933, when the Twenty-first Amendment repealed it. It is the only amendment ever repealed. It still matters because the court fights over its ratification set two rules for amending the Constitution: Congress can set a deadline for ratification, and a state referendum can't undo a legislature's vote to ratify. Key takeaways Passed by Congress December 18, 1917; ratified January 16, 1919. Repealed by the Twenty-first Amendment in 1933 . It banned manufacture, sale and transport "for beverage purposes." It didn't ban drinking itself . Congress enforced it through the Volstead Act, which covered drinks with as little as one-half of 1 percent alcohol . It was "the first to specify a deadline for its ratification": seven years . In Williams: today alcohol licensing belongs to the State of California, not the city .

Source: National Archives transcription Changed. Repealed. The Eighteenth Amendment was "Repealed by amendment 21," per the Archives. It is not law. Source: National Archives transcription Changed. Repealed. The Eighteenth Amendment was "Repealed by amendment 21," per the Archives. It is not law. Source: National Archives transcription Changed. Repealed. The Eighteenth Amendment was "Repealed by amendment 21," per

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: Section 1, the ban. After a one-year delay, it barred "the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors" in the U.S., plus importing and exporting them, "for beverage purposes" . Owning or drinking alcohol wasn't itself banned. Section 2, enforcement. "The Congress and the several States shall have concurrent power to enforce this article" . The Court read "concurrent power" so that it does "not mean joint power." Congress didn't need the states' approval to act . Section 3, deadline. The amendment would fail unless ratified "within seven years from the date of the submission hereof to the States by the Congress" .

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: By 1917, "the widespread proliferation of state restrictions on the liquor trade and Congress's enactment of wartime prohibition measures had laid the foundation for nationwide Prohibition" . Senator Morris Sheppard of Texas introduced the resolution on April 4, 1917, and the Senate approved it "on August 1, 1917" . Supporters argued that national enforcement would stop smuggling from "wet" states into "dry" ones. Opponents argued that federal policing of "individuals' social habits would intrude upon the states' reserved powers" . Senator Henry Cabot Lodge predicted Prohibition would be impossible to enforce and widely disobeyed . "Prohibition took effect throughout the United States on January 17, 1920." Congress had passed the Volstead Act in October 1919 . Fourteen years later, the Twenty-first Amendment repealed it. See Twenty-first Amendment .

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: National Prohibition Cases (1920). The Court upheld the amendment and the Volstead Act. A joint resolution passed "each by a two-thirds vote ... sufficiently shows that the proposal was deemed necessary by all who voted for it" ( National Prohibition Cases , 253 U.S. 350 (1920)) . It also held that Congress stayed within its enforcement power when the Volstead Act covered drinks with as little as one-half of 1 percent alcohol by volume . Hawke v. Smith (1920). Ohio voters tried to hold a referendum on the legislature's ratification. The Court said no: "ratification by a state of a constitutional amendment is not an act of legislation within the proper sense of the word. It is but the expression of the assent of the state to a proposed amendment" ( Hawke v. Smith , 253 U.S. 221 (1920)) . Dillon v. Gloss (1921). The Court upheld the seven-year deadline: "the ratification must be within some reasonable time after the proposal," and "Of the power of Congress, keeping within reasonable limits, to fix a definite period for the ratification we entertain no doubt" ( Dillon v. Gloss , 256 U.S. 368 (1921)) .

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: Our reading: the Eighteenth is the clearest example of an amendment used to set specific social policy rather than to structure government or protect rights. Its repeal shows that the Article V process works in both directions. Its court cases still govern how amendments are ratified. See Article V .

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: Today's rules come from the state. After repeal, California's constitution gave the state "the exclusive right and power to license and regulate the manufacture, sale, purchase, possession and transportation of alcoholic beverages within the State" (Art. XX, §22) . Bars, restaurants and stores in Williams get licenses from the state. The city's role is mostly land use. See Article XX . The drinking age is in the state constitution. "No person under the age of 21 years shall purchase any alcoholic beverage" (Art. XX, §22) . Referendums and amendments. Under Hawke , California voters couldn't use a referendum to reverse the Legislature's vote ratifying a federal amendment . Our reading: state initiatives can change California's own constitution, but not the ratification of a federal one. Local history. We haven't verified any public source on how Prohibition played out in Williams or Colusa County, so this lesson makes no claims about it.

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: "Prohibition made drinking illegal." The amendment banned manufacture, sale and transport for beverage purposes, not possession or drinking . "States could opt out." "Concurrent power" didn't mean states had to agree before federal enforcement took effect . "Voters could overturn their state's ratification by referendum." Hawke v. Smith rejected that . "Amendments never have deadlines." The Eighteenth was the first to set one, and the Court upheld it .

t: Eighteenth Amendment: Prohibition (repealed)
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. What repealed the Eighteenth Amendment? The Twenty-first Amendment, ratified December 5, 1933 . Did the Eighteenth Amendment ban drinking? No. It banned the manufacture, sale and transportation of intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes . Could Ohio voters undo the legislature's ratification by referendum? No. Hawke v. Smith held that ratification isn't ordinary legislation subject to referendum . Who licenses alcohol sales in Williams today? The State of California, under Article XX, §22 .

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: The Nineteenth Amendment says the right to vote can't be denied "on account of sex." Women had argued that the Fourteenth Amendment already protected their vote. In 1875 the Supreme Court disagreed, so it took a separate amendment, ratified in 1920. California figures in the story twice: a California senator first proposed the wording, and California voters gave women the vote in 1911, nine years before the nation did. Key takeaways Passed by Congress June 4, 1919; ratified August 18, 1920 . Same structure as the Fifteenth: neither the United States nor any state may deny the vote on this basis . Minor v. Happersett (1875) held citizenship "did not necessarily confer the right of suffrage" . First proposed in 1878 by Senator Aaron Sargent of California . California voters approved women's suffrage on October 10, 1911 . In Williams: it applies directly to every city, county, school and state election.

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: Official text Amendment XIX read in context : Amendment XIX The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex. Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: "Shall not be denied or abridged ... on account of sex." The amendment doesn't hand anyone the vote. It forbids using sex as a reason to deny or weaken it. The Court later said it "applies to men and women alike and by its own force supersedes inconsistent measures, whether federal or state" ( Breedlove v. Suttles , 302 U.S. 277 (1937)) . "By the United States or by any State." It binds every level of government, including cities, because cities act under state authority. Enforcement. "Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation" .

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: 1872: Susan B. Anthony. "In the 1872 presidential election, Susan B. Anthony cast a ballot in Rochester, New York. She was arrested and charged with illegally voting in violation of federal law" . A court fined her $100, "but she never paid it" . 1875: Minor v. Happersett . Virginia Minor sued after a Missouri registrar refused to register her. The Court held that "the Constitution, when it conferred citizenship, did not necessarily confer the right of suffrage" ( Minor v. Happersett , 88 U.S. 162 (1875)) . 1878: A California senator. "In 1878, Senator Aaron Sargent of California introduced a joint resolution proposing an amendment" barring restrictions on the vote "on account of sex" . Those words became the amendment's text. The western states move first. "A few western state governments accorded women full or partial voting rights," starting with the Territory of Wyoming in 1869 . 1911: California votes yes. The measure lost in the San Francisco Bay Area and "just barely passed in Los Angeles." Then "late reports from the rural counties began to swing the vote." The final count was "125,037 to 121,450, making California the 6th state in the nation to give women the right to vote" . 1917–1920: Congress, then the states. "In December 1917, Representative John E. Raker of California reintroduced the joint resolution" . Congress passed it in 1919, and it was ratified August 18,

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: Leser v. Garnett (1922). Maryland voters challenged the amendment. Ratification had been "proclaimed on August 26, 1920," and "The Legislature of Maryland had refused to ratify it" ( Leser v. Garnett , 258 U.S. 130 (1922)) . The Court compared it with the Fifteenth Amendment, adopted the same way: "One cannot be valid and the other invalid" . Breedlove v. Suttles (1937). This was "the only significant case addressing the Amendment's effect." The Court upheld a Georgia poll tax that exempted women who didn't register . The poll-tax part of Breedlove was later overruled. See Twenty-fourth Amendment . "Political equality." In striking down Georgia's county-unit vote system, the Court said the Nineteenth Amendment stands for "political equality" and illustrates "one person, one vote" .

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: Every local election. The amendment applies to Williams City Council races, local measures, and school and county elections, as well as state and federal ones. California's own rule. Article II, §2 of the state constitution says: "A United States citizen 18 years of age and resident in this State may vote" . Sex isn't part of the test. Equal districts locally. The one-person, one-vote principle reaches local governments. A government with "general governmental powers over an entire geographic area" can't use districts "of substantially unequal population" ( Avery v. Midland County , 390 U.S. 474 (1968)) . How Colusa County voted. The State Archives page says rural counties swung the 1911 vote . The official 1911 statement of vote shows Colusa County voters approved the suffrage amendment narrowly, 438 yes to 427 no . It reports counties, not towns, so it doesn't show how Williams itself voted.

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: "The Nineteenth gave all women the vote." It barred sex discrimination in voting. Other barriers, like poll taxes and literacy tests, kept many women (and men) from voting for decades afterward. See the Twenty-fourth Amendment . "Women couldn't vote anywhere before 1920." Wyoming, California and other states got there first . "It only protects women." It "applies to men and women alike" .

t: Nineteenth Amendment: Women's right to vote
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. Why didn't the Fourteenth Amendment already guarantee women the vote? Minor v. Happersett held citizenship did not necessarily include the right to vote . Who first proposed the "on account of sex" amendment in Congress? Senator Aaron Sargent of California, in 1878 . When did California voters approve women's suffrage? October 10, 1911, by 125,037 to 121,450 . What did Leser v. Garnett decide? It rejected challenges to the Nineteenth Amendment's ratification .

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: The Second Amendment has two parts: a prefatory clause about a "well regulated Militia" and an operative clause protecting "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms." For most of the 20th century its scope was unsettled. Since 2008 the Supreme Court has held it protects an individual right, since 2010 that it binds states and cities, and since 2022 that gun laws are judged by history rather than by balancing tests. Key takeaways An individual right, not only a right of militias ( Heller , 2008). Applies to states and cities ( McDonald , 2010). A gun law stands only if it's "consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" ( Bruen , 2022). Not unlimited: bans in "sensitive places" and disarming people found to be a credible threat are allowed ( Heller , Rahimi ). California's constitution has no right-to-bear-arms clause , so the federal amendment is the only constitutional protection here.

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: Official text Amendment II read in context : Amendment II A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State," is a prefatory clause. It announces a purpose but, per Heller , doesn't limit the right to militia service. "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed" is the operative clause. "Keep" means possess; "bear" means carry.

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008). "The Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess a firearm unconnected with service in a militia, and to use that arm for traditionally lawful purposes, such as self-defense within the home" ( District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570 (2008)) . The Court struck down D.C.'s handgun ban. It also listed "presumptively lawful" regulations, including "laws forbidding the carrying of firearms in sensitive places such as schools and government buildings, or laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms" . McDonald v. Chicago (2010). The Fourteenth Amendment "makes the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms fully applicable to the States" ( McDonald v. Chicago , 561 U.S. 742 (2010)) . Chicago's handgun ban fell. This is the case that makes the amendment a limit on Williams. New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn. v. Bruen (2022). The Court rejected the "two-step" approach lower courts had used. Now the government must "demonstrate that the regulation is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" ( New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn. v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1 (2022)) . New York's rule requiring "proper cause" for a carry license was struck down. The Court also warned that a city can't be declared a "sensitive place" just because it's crowded: "there is no historical basis for

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: Through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, since McDonald . A Williams ordinance on firearms must pass the Bruen history test. There's a second limit, from state law. California has a strong body of state gun law, and state law can preempt city ordinances that conflict with it or that enter a field the state fully occupies ( California Article XI, §7 ) . Our reading: a small general law city like Williams has little room to make its own gun rules beyond what state law already covers; check the specific Penal Code sections before assuming a city can act.

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: City buildings. A rule barring guns in City Hall or the council chamber fits Heller 's "government buildings" example . Parks and streets. A citywide ban on carrying in all public places would likely fail under Bruen . Discharge rules. Limits on firing guns within city limits are a common safety rule. This site hasn't checked the Williams Municipal Code for one, so don't assume.

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: "It only protects militias." Heller rejected that . "It only limits the federal government." McDonald applied it to states and cities . "Courts balance public safety against the right." Not since Bruen ; the test is history and tradition . "California's constitution protects gun rights too." It has no such clause.

t: Second Amendment: The right to keep and bear arms
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. What test does a gun law face after Bruen ? The government must show the regulation is "consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation" . Which case applied the Second Amendment to cities? McDonald v. Chicago (2010) . Name two kinds of regulation Heller called presumptively lawful. Bans on carrying in sensitive places such as schools and government buildings, and conditions on the commercial sale of arms (among others) .

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: Under the original schedule, newly elected officials waited until March 4 to take office. Defeated officials stayed in power for four months, and a Congress that had just been voted out could still meet and pass laws. The Twentieth Amendment shortened this "lame duck" period: Congress now starts January 3 and the President January 20. It also set rules for a President-elect who dies or can't take office. In Williams, newly elected council members take office once the council adopts the official election results. Key takeaways Passed by Congress March 2, 1932; ratified January 23, 1933. It modified Article I, §4 and superseded part of the Twelfth Amendment . President and Vice President's terms end at noon January 20; members of Congress at noon January 3 . Congress meets at least once a year, starting January 3 unless it sets another day by law . If the President-elect dies, the Vice President-elect becomes President. If neither qualifies, Congress decides who acts . In Williams: elected city officers serve from the installation after the council adopts the official canvass, "until their successors are elected and qualified" (Gov. Code §36503) .

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: Official text Amendment XX, Section 1 read in context : Amendment XX, Section 1 The terms of the President and Vice President shall end at noon on the 20th day of January, and the terms of Senators and Representatives at noon on the 3d day of January, of the years in which such terms would have ended if this article had not been ratified; and the terms of their successors shall then begin. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XX, Section 2 read in context : Amendment XX, Section 2 The Congress shall assemble at least once in every year, and such meeting shall begin at noon on the 3d day of January, unless they shall by law appoint a different day. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XX, Section 3 read in context : Amendment XX, Section 3 If, at the time fixed for the beginning of the term of the President, the President elect shall have died, the Vice President elect shall become President. If a President shall not have been chosen before the time fixed for the beginning of his term, or if the President elect shall have failed to qualify, then the Vice President elect shall act as President until a President shall have qualified; and the Congress may by law provide for the case wherein neither a President elect nor a Vice President elect shall have qualified, declaring who shall then act as President, or the manner in which

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: §1, end of terms. Terms of the President and Vice President end "at noon on the 20th day of January," and those of senators and representatives "at noon on the 3d day of January" . §2, annual meeting. "The Congress shall assemble at least once in every year," beginning January 3 "unless they shall by law appoint a different day." This replaced Article I, §4, clause 2 . §3, a President-elect who dies or isn't chosen. If the President-elect dies, "the Vice President elect shall become President." If no President has been chosen, or the President-elect "shall have failed to qualify," the Vice President-elect acts as President in the meantime. Congress may provide for the case where neither qualifies . §4, contingent elections. Congress can plan for a candidate's death while the House is choosing a President or the Senate a Vice President . See the Twelfth Amendment . §§5–6. §§1 and 2 took effect "on the 15th day of October following the ratification"; ratification had a seven-year deadline .

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: Congress first met under the Constitution on March 4, 1789. Terms ran from that date, so each new Congress and President started in March . Our reading: with elections in November, that meant four months in which officials who had lost could keep governing. Congress proposed the amendment on March 2, 1932, and "Ratification was completed on January 23, 1933, when the thirty-sixth state approved the amendment" . Getting to the new dates meant shortening some terms once. The amendment "in effect shortened the terms of the President and Vice President elected in 1932" by the gap between January 20 and March 4, 1937 . Some sitting senators' and representatives' terms were cut short by the January 3–March 4 gap too .

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: Acting under Section 3, "Congress passed the Presidential Succession Act of 1948," codified at 3 U.S.C. §19, for the case where neither the President-elect nor the Vice President-elect qualifies in time . For vacancies during a term, see the Twenty-fifth Amendment .

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: The Twentieth Amendment sets federal dates only. California law has its own version for city offices: When a new council member takes office. "City officers holding elective city office shall hold office for their prescribed terms from the date of the installation of officers following adoption by the council of the official canvass of their election and until their successors are elected and qualified" (Gov. Code §36503) . What that means in practice. After a November election, current members keep serving until results are certified and the new members are installed . The city's council page lists some terms ending "November 2026" . Watch the council agenda after the election for the canvass and swearing-in. See Agenda watch . What we couldn't verify. We haven't confirmed the exact date the Williams council will adopt the November 2026 canvass. It will appear on a posted agenda. Our reading: a new council can't vote until it's installed, so decisions made between Election Day and installation are made by the outgoing council. That's the same lame-duck gap the Twentieth Amendment narrowed for Congress.

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: "Inauguration was always in January." It was March 4 until the Twentieth Amendment; the first January 20 inauguration followed the 1936 election . "The 'lame duck' amendment ended lame-duck sessions." It shortened the gap. Congress can still meet after November elections before the new Congress starts on January 3. "Winners take office the day after the election." Federal officials take office on the dates in §1. Williams council members take office after the canvass is adopted .

t: Twentieth Amendment: Terms begin in January
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. When does a presidential term end? At noon on January 20 . What happens if the President-elect dies before inauguration? The Vice President-elect becomes President (§3) . Why were some terms shortened in the 1930s? Moving start dates from March 4 to January cut short terms already in progress, including those of the President and Vice President elected in 1932 . When does a newly elected Williams council member take office? At installation, after the council adopts the official canvass of the election (Gov. Code §36503) .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: The Twenty-first Amendment repealed Prohibition in 1933. Section 2 gave states broad power over alcohol coming across their borders, and that power still shapes liquor licensing. That power has limits, though: states can't use it to favor in-state businesses or to ignore the rest of the Constitution. In California, the state constitution gives alcohol licensing to the state, not to cities like Williams. Key takeaways Passed by Congress February 20, 1933; ratified December 5, 1933 . Section 1 repealed the Eighteenth Amendment . Section 2 bans bringing alcohol into a state in violation of that state's laws. It doesn't let states discriminate against out-of-state businesses . It's the only amendment ratified by state conventions, under Article V's alternate method . In Williams: alcohol licenses come from the State of California (Art. XX, §22), and the drinking age of 21 is in the state constitution .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: Official text Amendment XXI, Section 1 read in context : Amendment XXI, Section 1 The eighteenth article of amendment to the Constitution of the United States is hereby repealed. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXI, Section 2 read in context : Amendment XXI, Section 2 The transportation or importation into any State, Territory, or possession of the United States for delivery or use therein of intoxicating liquors, in violation of the laws thereof, is hereby prohibited. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXI, Section 3 read in context : Amendment XXI, Section 3 This article shall be inoperative unless it shall have been ratified as an amendment to the Constitution by conventions in the several States, as provided in the Constitution, within seven years from the date of the submission hereof to the States by the Congress. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: §1, repeal. "The eighteenth article of amendment to the Constitution of the United States is hereby repealed" . §2, state control. Transporting or importing liquor into a state "in violation of the laws thereof, is hereby prohibited" . Our reading: a state that stayed dry could rely on the Constitution itself to keep alcohol out. §3, conventions and a deadline. Ratification had to be "by conventions in the several States" within seven years .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: By the end of the "dry decade" of the 1920s, the Eighteenth Amendment "had failed to eliminate the illegal manufacture and sale of alcoholic beverages within the United States" . Repeal became a 1932 campaign issue: Franklin D. Roosevelt "openly supported the Eighteenth Amendment's repeal" . Congress proposed the amendment "on February 20, 1933." "On December 5, 1933, Acting Secretary of State William Phillips certified that the Amendment had been adopted by the requisite number of state conventions" .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: The Senate amended the joint resolution "to provide for its submission to specially elected delegates in state ratifying conventions rather than state legislatures" . Our reading: conventions let voters choose delegates on the single question of repeal, rather than leaving it to legislatures elected on many issues. See Article V .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: No favoring in-state businesses. Michigan and New York let in-state wineries ship directly to consumers but barred out-of-state wineries. "Both States' laws discriminate against interstate commerce in violation of the Commerce Clause, and that discrimination is neither authorized nor permitted by the Twenty-first Amendment" ( Granholm v. Heald , 544 U.S. 460 (2005)) . Tennessee's two-year residency rule for liquor store licenses "violates the Commerce Clause and is not saved by the Twenty-first Amendment" ( Tennessee Wine & Spirits Retailers Assn. v. Thomas , 588 U.S. 504 (2019)) . No exception to equal protection. Oklahoma allowed sales of 3.2% beer to women at 18 but to men only at 21. The Court struck down the law. In its summary of the ruling: "The Court has never recognized that application of that Amendment can defeat an otherwise established claim under the Equal Protection Clause" ( Craig v. Boren , 429 U.S. 190 (1976)) . How the drinking age became 21 everywhere. Congress didn't set a national drinking age. It withheld part of federal highway money from states that allowed drinking under 21. The Court upheld that: "encouragement to state action found in § 158 is a valid use of the spending power" ( South Dakota v. Dole , 483 U.S. 203 (1987)) .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: California's constitution gives the state "the exclusive right and power to license and regulate the manufacture, sale, purchase, possession and transportation of alcoholic beverages within the State" (Art. XX, §22) . It also says "no person under the age of 21 years shall purchase any alcoholic beverage" . See Article XX .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: Licenses come from the state. A bar, restaurant or store in Williams that sells alcohol is licensed by the State of California under Article XX, §22, not by the city . The city's role is land use. Cities generally regulate where businesses can operate through zoning and permits. See Planning . What we couldn't verify: we haven't reviewed the Williams Municipal Code for alcohol-specific zoning rules, so we make no claim about what they say. Check with the city's planning staff. Age 21. The rule against selling to or buying by anyone under 21 is in California's own constitution, separate from the federal highway-funding condition upheld in Dole .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: "Section 2 lets a state do anything with alcohol." It doesn't override the Commerce Clause or equal protection . "Congress passed a law making 21 the national drinking age." It used highway funding to encourage states to adopt 21 . "The city issues liquor licenses." In California the state does . "Repeal made alcohol legal everywhere." Repeal handed the question back to the states; §2 let dry states stay dry .

t: Twenty-first Amendment: Repeal of Prohibition
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. How was the Twenty-first Amendment ratified? By state ratifying conventions, the only amendment ratified that way . Can a state use Section 2 to protect in-state wineries from competition? No ( Granholm v. Heald ) . How did 21 become the drinking age in every state? Congress conditioned some highway funds on it, and South Dakota v. Dole upheld that . Who issues liquor licenses for businesses in Williams? The State of California, under Article XX, §22 .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: George Washington stepped down after two terms, and Presidents followed that custom until Franklin Roosevelt won four elections. The Twenty-second Amendment made the custom law: no one can be elected President more than twice. California sets its own term limits for state offices. A city council like Williams's has term limits only if the city's voters approve them. Key takeaways Passed by Congress March 21, 1947; ratified February 27, 1951 . No one can be elected President more than twice . Someone who served more than two years of another President's term can be elected only once. The most anyone can serve is ten years . "The Twenty-Second Amendment has yet to be applied" by a court, and some questions are still open . In Williams: under state law, council term limits apply only if city voters approve them at a regularly scheduled election .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: Official text Amendment XXII, Section 1 read in context : Amendment XXII, Section 1 No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice, and no person who has held the office of President, or acted as President, for more than two years of a term to which some other person was elected President shall be elected to the office of the President more than once. But this Article shall not apply to any person holding the office of President when this Article was proposed by the Congress, and shall not prevent any person who may be holding the office of President, or acting as President, during the term within which this Article becomes operative from holding the office of President or acting as President during the remainder of such term. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXII, Section 2 read in context : Amendment XXII, Section 2 This article shall be inoperative unless it shall have been ratified as an amendment to the Constitution by the legislatures of three-fourths of the several States within seven years from the date of its submission to the States by the Congress. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: "No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice." The limit is on elections , not years in office . Partial terms. Anyone who "has held the office of President, or acted as President, for more than two years of a term to which some other person was elected President" can be elected only once more . Our arithmetic: a Vice President who takes over with two years or less left can still be elected twice, for a total of up to ten years . Grandfather clause. It didn't apply to the President in office when it was proposed (Harry Truman) . Seven-year deadline. It had to be ratified within seven years, like the Eighteenth, Twentieth and Twenty-first .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: A 1947 House report described "a well-defined custom which has risen in the past that no President should have more than two terms in that office." The amendment was meant "to submit this question to the people" . That move "followed soon after the people had elected Franklin D. Roosevelt to unprecedented third and fourth terms of office, in 1940 and 1944, respectively" . Congress picked its words on purpose. Broader language saying a two-term President "shall be chosen or serve as President ... or be eligible to hold the office" was rejected "in favor of the Twenty-Second Amendment's ban merely on election" .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: Because the amendment bars only election, it "would not prevent someone who had twice been elected President from succeeding to the office after having been elected or appointed Vice President" . The catch is the Twelfth Amendment: "no person constitutionally ineligible to the office of President shall be eligible to that of Vice-President" . Is a two-term President "constitutionally ineligible"? No court has decided . See Twelfth Amendment .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: Legislators. "During her or his lifetime a person may serve no more than 12 years in the Senate, the Assembly, or both, in any combination of terms" (Art. IV, §2) . See Article IV . Governor. "No Governor may serve more than 2 terms" (Art. V, §2) . See Article V . Congress is different. States can't put term limits on their members of Congress. U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton held that state-by-state rules would be "inconsistent with the Framers' vision of a uniform National Legislature" ( U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton , 514 U.S. 779 (1995)) .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: No federal limit on council terms. The Twenty-second Amendment covers only the presidency. How a city adopts council term limits. State law lets "the city council of a general law or charter city" adopt, or residents propose "by initiative," a limit on council terms or an elected mayor's terms. A limit "shall apply prospectively only" and needs a majority of voters "at a regularly scheduled election" (Gov. Code §36502(b)) . Williams is a general law city . What the city's guide says. The 2026 candidate guide says council members "serve a 4 year term" and doesn't mention any term limit . What we couldn't verify. We haven't found a Williams ordinance or ballot measure limiting council terms. A guide that doesn't mention one isn't proof there is none; ask the City Clerk before assuming either way. Staggered terms. The city's council page lists some members' terms ending November 2026 and others November 2028, so seats come up in different election years .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: "A President can never serve more than eight years." Someone who finishes two years or less of another's term can still be elected twice . "Term limits were in the original Constitution." Two terms was only a custom until 1951 . "States can term-limit their members of Congress." Thornton says no . "The council can impose term limits on its own vote." Under §36502(b), voters must approve them .

t: Twenty-second Amendment: Presidential term limits
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. What is the maximum time someone can serve as President? Ten years: up to two years of a predecessor's term plus two elected terms . What prompted the amendment? Franklin Roosevelt's election to third and fourth terms . How many years can a person serve in the California Legislature? No more than 12 in the Senate, Assembly, or both (Art. IV, §2) . Can Williams limit council terms? Yes, but only if city voters approve it at a regularly scheduled election, and it applies only going forward (Gov. Code §36502(b)) .

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x: Washington, D.C. isn't a state, so under Article II it had no presidential electors and its residents had no vote for President. The Twenty-third Amendment, ratified in 1961, gave the District electors, capped at the number held by the smallest state. It did nothing else: D.C. still has no voting members of Congress. The lesson for a Williams resident is that your voting rights depend on where you legally live, and that is just as true at the city line as at the state line. Key takeaways Passed by Congress June 16, 1960; ratified March 29, 1961 . D.C. gets the electors it would have as a state, but never more than the least populous state. Today that works out to 3 . D.C.'s electors count as if a state appointed them and follow the Twelfth Amendment's voting rules. It doesn't make D.C. a state or give it voting members of Congress . In Williams: you vote in city elections only if you live inside the city limits. A neighbor a mile outside town votes for county supervisor, not for the Williams council .

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x: Official text Amendment XXIII, Section 1 read in context : Amendment XXIII, Section 1 The District constituting the seat of Government of the United States shall appoint in such manner as the Congress may direct: A number of electors of President and Vice President equal to the whole number of Senators and Representatives in Congress to which the District would be entitled if it were a State, but in no event more than the least populous State; they shall be in addition to those appointed by the States, but they shall be considered, for the purposes of the election of President and Vice President, to be electors appointed by a State; and they shall meet in the District and perform such duties as provided by the twelfth article of amendment. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXIII, Section 2 read in context : Amendment XXIII, Section 2 The Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
s: What it does, clause by clause
x: "The District constituting the seat of Government ... shall appoint." The District, not a state, picks electors, "in such manner as the Congress may direct" . Congress, not a state legislature, writes the rules. How many. "A number of electors ... equal to the whole number of Senators and Representatives in Congress to which the District would be entitled if it were a State, but in no event more than the least populous State" . Counted like a state's. D.C.'s electors "shall be considered, for the purposes of the election of President and Vice President, to be electors appointed by a State," and they "meet in the District and perform such duties as provided by the twelfth article of amendment" . See the Twelfth Amendment . Section 2. Congress can enforce it "by appropriate legislation" .

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x: Article II gives each state electors "equal to the whole Number of Senators and Representatives to which the State may be entitled in the Congress," and Article I guarantees every state "at Least one Representative" . So the least populous state has two senators plus one representative: 3 electors. D.C. would have more if it were counted like a state by population, but the cap holds it to 3 .

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x: The Constitution put the national capital in a federal "District (not exceeding ten Miles square)" under Congress's control (Art. I, §8) . Its residents were not part of any state, so they had no electors. The House committee report on the amendment said it would "provide the citizens of the District of Columbia with appropriate rights of voting in national elections for President and Vice President of the United States" . The report was just as clear about the limits. The amendment "would change the Constitution only to the minimum extent necessary," and "It would not make the District of Columbia a State" . It would not "change the constitutional powers of the Congress to legislate with respect to the District of Columbia and to prescribe its form of government" .

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
s: Electors after the votes are counted
x: When you vote for President, you are really choosing your state's electors. The Supreme Court described it this way: "every State appoints a slate of electors selected by the political party whose candidate has won the State's popular vote" (with two partial exceptions) . Can an elector break a pledge and vote for someone else? In Chiafalo v. Washington (2020), three Washington electors who did so challenged the fines they received. The Court upheld the state's law, noting that "32 States and the District of Columbia" have statutes meant to prevent "faithless voting" ( Chiafalo v. Washington , 591 U.S. 578 (2020)) . The District is on that list. That fits the amendment's design: D.C.'s electors are treated as if a state had appointed them.

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x: The Twenty-third Amendment doesn't touch Williams directly. Its theme does: your vote depends on where you legally live. City elections are for city residents. A qualified voter "may vote at any election held within the territory within which he or she resides and the election is held" (Elections Code §2000) . Someone living in unincorporated Colusa County just outside town can't vote for the Williams City Council, even if they shop, work or pay utility bills in town. Our reading: that's the D.C. problem at local scale. Annexation (moving the city line) changes who gets a vote. Running for council works the same way. A council candidate must be "an elector of the city" when taking office, and if a council member moves "outside of the city limits ... his or her office shall immediately become vacant" (Gov. Code §36502) . Williams in a presidential year. Williams voters help choose California's electors. California has two senators plus its House seats, the same Article II formula that sets D.C.'s cap . See Article II . We have not found any Williams- or Colusa-specific history connected to this amendment.

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x: "The Twenty-third Amendment made D.C. a state." The House report says outright that it "would not make the District of Columbia a State" . "D.C. has a voting member of Congress." The amendment covers only presidential electors . "D.C.'s electors are based on its population." Population is the starting point, but the number can never be more than the least populous state's . "Anyone near Williams can vote in city elections." Only people who live inside the city limits can .

t: Twenty-third Amendment: Electoral votes for Washington, D.C.
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. How many electors can D.C. have at most? No more than the least populous state, which today means 3 . Does the Twenty-third Amendment give D.C. a voting member of the House? No. It only covers presidential electors . Who decides how D.C. picks its electors? Congress: the District appoints them "in such manner as the Congress may direct" . Can someone who lives just outside the Williams city limits vote for the city council? No. Voters vote in elections held "within the territory within which he or she resides" (Elections Code §2000) .

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: A poll tax is a flat fee you had to pay before you could vote. Along with literacy tests, poll taxes kept many poor and Black citizens from the polls. The Twenty-fourth Amendment banned them in federal elections in 1964. Two years later, the Supreme Court used the Fourteenth Amendment to ban them in state and local elections too. Today no one can be charged to vote in any election, Williams City Council races included. Key takeaways Passed by Congress August 27, 1962; ratified January 23, 1964 . It covers elections for President, Vice President, Senate and House, including primaries . No "equivalent or milder substitute" may be imposed ( Harman , 1965) . For state and city elections, Harper (1966) bars any wealth or fee requirement under the Fourteenth Amendment . In Williams: voting in a city election can't depend on paying any fee or tax .

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: Official text Amendment XXIV, Section 1 read in context : Amendment XXIV, Section 1 The right of citizens of the United States to vote in any primary or other election for President or Vice President, for electors for President or Vice President, or for Senator or Representative in Congress, shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any State by reason of failure to pay any poll tax or other tax. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXIV, Section 2 read in context : Amendment XXIV, Section 2 The Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: "In any primary or other election." Primaries count, not just November general elections . Federal offices only. It names elections for "President or Vice President, for electors for President or Vice President, or for Senator or Representative in Congress" . State and local elections came later, through Harper . "Any poll tax or other tax." Not just a poll tax: no tax of any kind may be a condition of voting in these elections . Section 2. Congress may enforce it .

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: "Property qualifications extend back to colonial days, but the poll tax itself as a qualification was instituted in eleven states of the South following the end of Reconstruction." By ratification in 1964, "only five states still retained it" . Ratification was "the culmination of an endeavor begun in Congress in 1939." Congress saw the tax as "an obstacle to the proper exercise of a citizen's franchise" .

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: Breedlove v. Suttles (1937). The Court upheld Georgia's "poll tax of one dollar," which exempted "females who do not register for voting" ( Breedlove v. Suttles , 302 U.S. 277 (1937)) . Harman v. Forssenius (1965). Virginia gave federal voters a choice: pay the poll tax or file a certificate of residence six months before the election. The Court struck it down: "For federal elections, the poll tax is abolished absolutely as a prerequisite to voting, and no equivalent or milder substitute may be imposed" ( Harman v. Forssenius , 380 U.S. 528 (1965)) . Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966). "A State violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment whenever it makes the affluence of the voter or payment of any fee an electoral standard. Voter qualifications have no relation to wealth nor to paying or not paying this or any other tax" ( Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections , 383 U.S. 663 (1966)) . The Court said this holds "whether the citizen, otherwise qualified to vote, has $1.50 in his pocket or nothing at all," and "To that extent the Breedlove case is overruled" .

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: No fee to vote, ever. No city, county or state election in Williams can charge voters or require them to be paid up on any tax . That covers council races and local tax measures. California's qualifications don't involve money. "A United States citizen 18 years of age and resident in this State may vote" (Art. II, §2) . And "A voter who casts a vote in an election in accordance with the laws of this State shall have that vote counted" (Art. II, §2.5) . See California Article II . Owing the city money doesn't matter. Our reading: under Harper , a resident behind on a utility bill or city fee can still vote. Paying a tax can't be an "electoral standard" . Different questions. Filing fees for candidates and fees for city services aren't covered by this amendment or by Harper 's voter rule. See City fees .

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: "The Twenty-fourth Amendment covers city elections." Its text covers only federal elections. Harper covers state and local ones . "A small fee is fine." Harper barred "payment of any fee," and Harman barred even a "milder substitute" in federal elections . "Poll taxes were only about race." They also kept poor voters of every race from voting. Harper rests on wealth discrimination .

t: Twenty-fourth Amendment: No poll taxes in federal elections
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. Does the Twenty-fourth Amendment itself cover city council elections? No, only federal elections. Harper covers state and local elections under equal protection . Could Virginia offer a residence certificate as an alternative to the poll tax in federal elections? No. Harman barred any equivalent or milder substitute . Which case did Harper overrule? Breedlove v. Suttles (1937), to the extent it upheld poll taxes . Can someone behind on a city bill be kept from voting in Williams? No. Payment of any fee or tax can't be a voting qualification .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: The original Constitution was unclear on three things. When a President died, did the Vice President become President or only act as one? How was an empty vice presidency filled? And what happened if a President became disabled? The Twenty-fifth Amendment answers all three. Sections 1 through 3 have all been used. Section 4, the contested-disability procedure, never has. California's constitution has close parallels, and Williams has its own rule for an empty council seat. Key takeaways Passed by Congress July 6, 1965; ratified February 10, 1967 . §1. If the President is removed, dies or resigns, the Vice President becomes President . §2. A vacant vice presidency is filled by the President's nominee, confirmed by a majority vote of both houses . §3. The President can voluntarily hand power to the Vice President as Acting President, for example during surgery . §4. The Vice President and a majority of the Cabinet can declare the President unable to serve, and Congress resolves any dispute. It "has never been used" . In Williams: a vacant council seat must be filled by appointment or a special-election call within 60 days .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: Official text Amendment XXV, Section 1 read in context : Amendment XXV, Section 1 In case of the removal of the President from office or of his death or resignation, the Vice President shall become President. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXV, Section 2 read in context : Amendment XXV, Section 2 Whenever there is a vacancy in the office of the Vice President, the President shall nominate a Vice President who shall take office upon confirmation by a majority vote of both Houses of Congress. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXV, Section 3 read in context : Amendment XXV, Section 3 Whenever the President transmits to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives his written declaration that he is unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office, and until he transmits to them a written declaration to the contrary, such powers and duties shall be discharged by the Vice President as Acting President. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXV, Section 4 read in context : Amendment XXV, Section 4 Whenever the Vice President and a majority of either the principal officers of the executive departments or of such other body as Congress may by law provide, transmit to the President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representati

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: Article II said the President's powers and duties "shall devolve on the Vice President," which left unclear whether the Vice President took over the office itself . "President John Tyler had established, as a matter of historical precedent, that the full office of the President, rather than only the President's 'powers and duties,' would devolve upon the Vice President in the event of the President's death" . Section 1 wrote that precedent down. There was also no way to fill a vacant vice presidency. Before 1967, "the vice presidency was vacant 16 times for a total of more than 37 years" . And Presidents had been disabled with no clear process: James Garfield "survived for 80 days after an assassin shot him"; Woodrow Wilson "suffered a stroke and was incapacitated for a significant part of his second term" .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: §2, 1973. After Vice President Spiro Agnew resigned, President Nixon nominated Gerald Ford, and Congress confirmed him "by a vote of 92 to 3" in the Senate and "387 to 35" in the House . §1, 1974. "President Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974," and "Vice President Ford immediately became President by operation of Section 1" . Ford then used §2 to fill his own former office, choosing Nelson Rockefeller . §3. "President Ronald Reagan implicitly invoked Section 3" during colon cancer surgery in 1985. Presidents George W. Bush and Joe Biden later used it during routine colonoscopies . §4. Never invoked .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: If the President disputes a declaration of inability, the conferees who wrote the final version chose "a four-day deadline for the Vice President (as Acting President) and Cabinet (or other body) to challenge a President's recovery declaration under Section 4; ... a 48-hour deadline for Congress to assemble (if not in session) after the relevant officials challenge the President's recovery declaration; and ... a 21-day deadline for Congress to decide" . Keeping the President out requires two-thirds of both houses .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: Governor. "The Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of Governor," and acts as Governor during "the impeachment, absence from the State, or other temporary disability of the Governor" (Art. V, §10) . Who decides disputes. "The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to determine all questions arising under this section" . Our reading: California gives disability disputes to its Supreme Court. The federal amendment gives them to Congress. Filling statewide offices. When the Lieutenant Governor's office or another statewide office is vacant, "the Governor shall nominate a person to fill the vacancy who shall take office upon confirmation by a majority of the membership of the Senate and a majority of the membership of the Assembly" (Art. V, §5(b)) . That is the same idea as federal §2. See California Article V .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: A vacant council seat. The council "shall, within 60 days from the commencement of the vacancy, either fill the vacancy by appointment or call a special election to fill the vacancy" (Gov. Code §36512) . An appointee's term depends on when the vacancy happens relative to the next general municipal election . Moving away creates a vacancy. If a council member "moves his or her place of residence outside of the city limits," the "office shall immediately become vacant" (Gov. Code §36502(a)) . How Williams picks its mayor. Voters don't elect the mayor directly. The city's 2026 candidate guide says the "City Council appoints the Mayor and Mayor Pro Tem at the first meeting of the year" , and the November 3, 2026 city ballot lists only three council seats and City Treasurer, no mayor's office . What we couldn't verify. We haven't found the city's written rules for when a mayor pro tem fills in. Ask the City Clerk for the local procedure .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: "The Cabinet can remove a President." Section 4 suspends the President's powers temporarily; if the President disagrees, Congress decides, and keeping the President out takes two-thirds of both houses . Removal from office still requires impeachment. "Section 4 has been used." It never has . "An appointed Vice President has never become President." Gerald Ford did, in 1974 . "A vacant council seat waits for the next election." The council must act within 60 days .

t: Twenty-fifth Amendment: Presidential succession and disability
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. Under §1, does the Vice President "act as" or "become" President when the President dies? Becomes President . Who confirms a new Vice President under §2? A majority vote of both houses of Congress . How large a vote does Congress need to keep a disputing President out of power under §4? Two-thirds of both houses . Who decides disputes about the California Governor's disability? The California Supreme Court (Art. V, §10) .

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: The Twenty-sixth Amendment says citizens 18 and older can't be denied the vote "on account of age." It took about three months to ratify, after the Supreme Court split on whether Congress could lower the voting age by statute. It applies to every election, Williams City Council races included. In California, 16- and 17-year-olds can preregister so they're ready to vote at 18. Key takeaways Passed by Congress March 23, 1971; ratified July 1, 1971. It replaced the "twenty-one" in Fourteenth Amendment §2 . It covers every election: federal, state and local. It followed Oregon v. Mitchell (1970), which let Congress set 18 for federal elections but not state and local ones . The California Supreme Court enforced it in 1971, ruling that 18-to-20-year-olds can register where they actually live . In Williams: a 16- or 17-year-old can preregister, and anyone who will be 18 by the next election can register for it .

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: Official text Amendment XXVI, Section 1 read in context : Amendment XXVI, Section 1 The right of citizens of the United States, who are eighteen years of age or older, to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of age. Source: National Archives transcription Official text Amendment XXVI, Section 2 read in context : Amendment XXVI, Section 2 The Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: "Citizens of the United States, who are eighteen years of age or older." It sets a floor. A state may not shut out voters 18 and older because of age . "Shall not be denied or abridged." "Abridged" means weakened, not just denied. Courts have used it against rules that made voting harder for young people (see below). "By the United States or by any State." The same words as the Fifteenth and Nineteenth Amendments, so it reaches local elections too . Section 2. Congress may enforce it. Federal law lets the Justice Department sue state and local governments that violate it .

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: World War II. Congress lowered the draft age to 18. That led some officials to ask why 18- to 20-year-old servicemembers couldn't vote, and the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote" caught on . Korea and Vietnam. Support grew "as Americans questioned why young soldiers fighting in Korea and Vietnam could not exercise the franchise" . 1970: a statute and a split Court. Congress "lowered the minimum voting age to 18 in federal elections—but not state elections—by enacting the Voting Rights Act Amendments of 1970" . The 1970 law tried to cover all elections. In Oregon v. Mitchell , the deciding opinion said Congress could "enfranchise 18-year-old citizens in national elections" but "cannot set the voting age in state and local elections" ( Oregon v. Mitchell , 400 U.S. 112 (1970)) . 1971: about three months. Congress sent the amendment to the states "on March 23, 1971," and it was ratified July 1 . President Nixon said the "11 million new young voters" would bring "a spirit of moral courage" to the electorate .

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: "The Supreme Court has not decided any cases definitively interpreting the Twenty-Sixth Amendment" . Other courts have: Jolicoeur v. Mihaly (California Supreme Court, 1971). State officials "violated the Twenty-Sixth Amendment when they treated unmarried 'minor' citizens of at least 18 years of age who did not live with their parents 'differently from adults' for voting purposes." They had refused to let these young voters register where they actually lived . Our reading: a college student or young worker who has moved out can register at their own address, the same as any adult. Texas residency rules. A federal court struck down rules that set voting residency for people under 21 "on a different basis than persons twenty-one years of age and older" .

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: City elections are included. Any U.S. citizen 18 or older who lives in Williams and is registered can vote for City Council and on local measures. California's constitution says: "A United States citizen 18 years of age and resident in this State may vote" (Art. II, §2(a)) . Preregister at 16. A person may preregister if they are a citizen, a California resident, not imprisoned for a felony, "and at least 16 years of age" (Elections Code §2101(b)) . To register to vote, you must be "at least 18 years of age at the time of the next election" (§2101(a)) . Deadline. A registration counts if the county elections official gets it "on or before the 15th day before an election," including through the Secretary of State's website . Colusa County runs registration and elections for Williams . Where you live counts. You vote where you reside, so a young adult who moved out of a parent's home in another town can register in Williams (see Jolicoeur above) .

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: "It only covers federal elections." That was the 1970 statute after Oregon v. Mitchell . The amendment covers every election . "Students have to vote where their parents live." Jolicoeur rejected treating 18-to-20-year-olds differently from other adults on residence . "You can't do anything until you turn 18." In California you can preregister at 16 . "The amendment bans all age limits." It protects those 18 and older. It doesn't require letting younger people vote.

t: Twenty-sixth Amendment: Voting at 18
x: Answer in your head first, then open each question. What did Oregon v. Mitchell decide about the 1970 law? Congress could set 18 as the voting age for federal elections but not for state and local elections . Does the Twenty-sixth Amendment apply to a Williams City Council election? Yes. It binds the United States and every state, including in local elections . At what age can a Californian preregister to vote? 16 (Elections Code §2101(b)) . What did the California Supreme Court decide in Jolicoeur v. Mihaly ? Young adults 18 and older who live on their own must be allowed to register where they actually live, like other adults .

t: Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
x: The Twenty-seventh Amendment says a law changing what members of Congress are paid can't take effect "until an election of Representatives shall have intervened." It was proposed in 1789 with what became the Bill of Rights and wasn't ratified until 1992, more than two centuries later. California applies the same idea to city councils: a council member can't get a raise during the term in which it was voted. Key takeaways Originally proposed September 25, 1789; ratified May 7, 1992 . A pay raise or cut for Congress waits until after the next House election . It had no ratification deadline, which is why it could become law so late . "The Supreme Court has not decided any cases interpreting the Twenty-Seventh Amendment" . In Williams: "A change in compensation does not apply to a council member during the council member's term of office" (Gov. Code §36516.5) .

t: Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
x: Official text Amendment XXVII read in context : Amendment XXVII No law, varying the compensation for the services of the Senators and Representatives, shall take effect, until an election of Representatives shall have intervened. Source: National Archives transcription

t: Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
x: "Varying the compensation." It covers raises and cuts alike . "Shall take effect, until an election of Representatives shall have intervened." Congress can pass a pay change at any time, but it can't take effect until after the next House election. Voters get a chance to respond first . What it doesn't do. It doesn't set an amount or ban raises. Congress still sets its own pay under Article I, §6 .

t: Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
x: 1789. "The original Constitution, which took effect in 1789, did not prevent federal laws that increased or decreased Members of Congress' salaries from becoming operative before the next congressional election" . During ratification, critics worried Congress could "indulge themselves in the fullest extent" by setting their pay "as high as they please" . The First Congress proposed this amendment along with the ten that became the Bill of Rights . Stalled. "By the end of 1791, only six of the then-existing fourteen states had ratified the Pay Amendment" . A college paper. "In 1982, Gregory D. Watson, an undergraduate student at the University of Texas at Austin, wrote about the Congressional Pay Amendment in a paper for a political science class." He argued it was still pending because Congress had set no deadline . "From the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, more than 30 state legislatures ratified the Amendment" . 1992. "On May 18, 1992, National Archivist Don W. Wilson ... proclaimed the Amendment to have been ratified on May 7, 1992" .

t: Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
x: In Dillon v. Gloss (1921), the Court said "the ratification must be within some reasonable time after the proposal" and should be "sufficiently contemporaneous" across states ( Dillon v. Gloss , 256 U.S. 368 (1921)) . In Coleman v. Miller (1939), however, the Court treated timeliness as "a political question pertaining to the political departments, with the ultimate authority in the Congress" ( Coleman v. Miller , 307 U.S. 433 (1939)) . The Twenty-seventh was accepted as ratified after more than 200 years. See Article V .

t: Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
x: Cost-of-living adjustments. In Boehner v. Anderson (1994), a federal appeals court "rejected a Twenty-Seventh Amendment challenge to congressional pay legislation." Congressman John Boehner had challenged automatic adjustments under the Ethics Reform Act of 1989 . Untested ideas. "It is unclear whether various novel statutory mechanisms for regulating Members' pay might comply with the Twenty-Seventh Amendment," such as the 2013 "No Budget, No Pay Act," which would have temporarily withheld members' pay until their chamber agreed to a budget resolution .

t: Twenty-seventh Amendment: Congressional pay
x: The amendment covers only Congress. California has parallel rules for city councils in general law cities like Williams : No mid-term raises. "A change in compensation does not apply to a council member during the council member's term of office." There's an exception for councils with staggered terms: when one member starts a new term, all members' pay can be adjusted (Gov. Code §36516.5) . Williams has staggered terms; the city lists some seats ending November 2026 and others November 2028 . Caps and process. A council may set salaries by ordinance. For cities of up to 35,000 people, the cap is "nine hundred fifty dollars ($950) per month," and raises above that are limited to set yearly amounts . "No ordinance shall be enacted or amended to provide automatic future increases in salary" (§36516(a)(5)) . Voters can decide instead. Whether council members get a salary, and how much, can also be put to voters at a municipal election (§36516(b)) . What Williams pays. The city's 2026 candidate guide says: "Councilmembers receive a monthly stipend of $420 and the Mayor receives $560" . Williams had an estimated 5,621 residents on January 1, 2026 , so the $950-a-month cap for cities of up to 35,000 applies . What we couldn't verify. We haven't read the ordinance that set those amounts. Ask the City Clerk for it. Our reading: unlike the federal rule, California's version bans automat

x: "It bans congressional raises." It only delays them until after a House election . "It's a modern amendment." It was written in 1789 and ratified in 1992 . "Amendments expire if they aren't ratified quickly." Only if Congress sets a deadline. This one had none . "A city council can vote itself an immediate raise." In California, a pay change doesn't apply during the member's current term .

Miller say about how long ratification can take? Timeliness is a political question for Congress . Who revived the amendment in the 1980s? Gregory D.
