t: Glossary
x: Plain-language meanings of words used on this site. Many are general definitions written by volunteers and labeled ; where a definition quotes a constitution or statute we read, it is labeled . Unofficial education, not legal advice.

t: Glossary
Glossary
x: The list of items a public body will discuss at a meeting. Under the Brown Act, a regular meeting's agenda must be posted at least 72 hours ahead .

t: Glossary
x: The agenda plus the staff reports and documents for each item. Williams posts packets as PDFs; many older ones are scanned images .

t: Glossary
x: A change added to a constitution. The U.S. Constitution has 27 amendments .

t: Glossary
x: The rule that the federal government can't order states, or their cities and counties, to enact or enforce a federal regulatory program ( Printz ) .

t: Glossary
x: An argument that a law was used unconstitutionally on particular facts, as opposed to a facial challenge, which says the words themselves are invalid in every case. Our explanation, not a quote .

t: Glossary
x: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, including freedom of speech and assembly (First Amendment) and protection from unreasonable searches (Fourth Amendment) .

t: Glossary
x: California's open-meetings law for local bodies such as a city council (Gov. Code §54950 and following) . See the Brown Act guide .

t: Glossary
x: The state law that lets anyone ask for records held by public agencies (Gov. Code §7920.000 and following) . See the Public Records Act guide .

t: Glossary
x: Law made by court decisions. The holding is the part of a decision that answers the legal question; it is what later courts follow .

t: Glossary
x: A California city with its own charter, a kind of local constitution, which gives it more control over its own municipal affairs. Williams is not a charter city .

t: Glossary
x: A part of a meeting closed to the public, allowed only for topics the Brown Act lists, such as some personnel matters, labor negotiations, litigation and real estate .

t: Glossary
x: The last ordinance that has been added to the published code. A search snippet says the official Williams code on Municode is codified through Ordinance 275-25 (December 10, 2025) . Newer ordinances may not appear yet.

t: Glossary
x: The founding law of a country or state. It sets up the government and limits its power. Both the U.S. and California have one .

t: Glossary
x: A change so broad it alters the basic plan of the California Constitution. Voters can amend the constitution by initiative but can't revise it that way; revisions go through the Legislature or a convention (Art. XVIII) .

t: Glossary
x: A written demand asking a public body to undo an action taken in violation of certain Brown Act rules. It must be sent within 90 days of the action (30 days for some agenda violations) (Gov. Code §54960.1) .

t: Glossary
x: The Fourteenth Amendment says no state shall “deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law” . In plain terms: fair procedures, such as notice and a chance to be heard, and laws clear enough to follow .

t: Glossary
x: The Fourteenth Amendment says no state shall “deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws” ; the California Constitution has a similar rule (Art. I, §7) . In plain terms: the government must have a valid reason to treat people differently .

t: Glossary
x: A fine so out of proportion to the offense that the Constitution forbids it. The Eighth Amendment and Art. I, §17 of the California Constitution both ban excessive fines, and the federal ban applies to cities . A fine is unconstitutional if it is "grossly disproportional to the gravity of the offense" . See the Williams page .

t: Glossary
x: When the state has covered a subject so fully that there is no room left for local rules, even ones that do not directly contradict state law .

t: Glossary
x: A California city without its own charter, so it runs under the state's general laws. The city says Williams “was made a General Law City on May 20, 1920” .

t: Glossary
x: State laws that apply across California. City ordinances may not be “in conflict with general laws” (Cal. Const., Art. XI, §7) . Which state laws count as “general laws” can be a hard legal question .

t: Glossary
x: A local tax for general government purposes. A city can impose, extend or increase one only with a majority vote of the electorate (Art. XIII C, §2(b)) .

t: Glossary
x: Giving public money or property to a private party without a public purpose, which Article XVI, §6 of the California Constitution forbids .

t: Glossary
x: One of California's collections of state statutes. It includes the Brown Act and the Public Records Act .

t: Glossary
x: What a court actually decided on the facts before it. The rest of an opinion explains the decision. Later courts follow holdings. Our explanation, not a quote .

t: Glossary
x: How the Bill of Rights came to limit states and cities. It first applied only to the federal government; through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, courts have applied almost all of it to the states . See how it happened .

t: Glossary
x: A minor violation, usually punished by a fine and not by jail . Check the code section and its penalty chapter for what applies.

t: Glossary
x: A way for voters to propose a new ordinance by petition. A city initiative petition needs signatures of 10% of registered voters; the council must then adopt it, put it on the ballot, or order a report first (Elec. Code §9215) .

t: Glossary
x: A court order, "signed by a judge of a court of record," that lets an official inspect property for code compliance . Outside emergencies, an inspector without consent generally needs one . See entry and inspection .

t: Glossary
x: The area or subjects over which a government body or court has authority .

t: Glossary
x: A crime more serious than an infraction and less serious than a felony; it can carry jail time .

t: Glossary
x: The Williams Municipal Code: the city's ordinances, organized by title and chapter. The official version is on Municode .

t: Glossary
x: The oath every California public officer and employee takes to support and defend the U.S. and California constitutions (Art. XX, §3) .

t: Glossary
x: A local law adopted by the City Council. Most ordinances become part of the municipal code .

t: Glossary
x: A government's general power to make rules for public health, safety and welfare. The California Constitution lets a city make “local, police, sanitary, and other ordinances” that do not conflict with general laws (Art. XI, §7) .

t: Glossary
x: When a higher law displaces a lower one. California courts have said a local rule conflicts with state law when it duplicates it, contradicts it, or enters a field the state fully occupies . See Three layers of law .

t: Glossary
x: A fee or charge "imposed by an agency upon a parcel or upon a person as an incident of property ownership, including a user fee or charge for a property-related service" (Cal. Const., Art. XIII D, §2(e)). A new or higher one needs mailed notice, a hearing at least 45 days later, and fails if a majority of affected owners protest in writing (§6(a)) . See Proposition 218 .

t: Glossary
x: Time at a meeting when members of the public may speak. The council must allow it on matters within its jurisdiction, may set reasonable time limits, and may not prohibit criticism (Gov. Code §54954.3) .

t: Glossary
x: A writing about the public's business kept by a public agency. The California Constitution says “the writings of public officials and agencies shall be open to public scrutiny” (Art. I, §3(b)(1)) ; the Public Records Act sets the details and exemptions .

t: Glossary
x: The rule that the state holds navigable waters and tidelands in trust for the public. California courts say it protects navigable waters from harm caused by diverting their tributaries ( National Audubon ) .

t: Glossary
x: "Recall is the power of the electors to remove an elective officer" (Cal. Const., Art. II, §13) . For city officers, the signatures needed depend on the number of registered voters (Elec. Code §11221) . See recalling a city officer .

t: Glossary
x: A way for voters to challenge a new ordinance. The petition must be filed within 30 days after the ordinance is adopted, signed by 10% of the city's registered voters; the council must then repeal it or put it to a vote (Elec. Code §9237) .

t: Glossary
x: A formal council decision that is not an ordinance. Budgets, many fees and many contracts are adopted by resolution, and a referendum does not apply to resolutions .

t: Glossary
x: The federal law (42 U.S.C. §1983) that lets people sue state and local officials, and cities, for violating federal constitutional rights. A city is liable for its own policy or custom ( Monell ) .

t: Glossary
x: Enforcing a law against some people and not others. Ordinary unevenness is not a constitutional violation; "deliberate invidious discrimination" in enforcement is, and can be raised as a defense . See charging discretion .

t: Glossary
x: A local tax for a specific purpose. It needs approval by a two-thirds vote of the electorate (Art. XIII C, §2(d)) .

t: Glossary
x: A memo from city staff in the agenda packet explaining an item, usually with a recommendation and its cost (“fiscal impact”) .

t: Glossary
x: A law passed by a legislature: Congress for federal law, the California Legislature for state law . Read California statutes on leginfo .

t: Glossary
x: Article VI of the U.S. Constitution: the Constitution and federal laws made under it are “the supreme Law of the Land,” binding state judges even if state law says otherwise .

t: Glossary
x: When government takes private property for public use, it must pay "just compensation" (Fifth Amendment). California adds property "damaged" and requires payment first (Art. I, §19) . Keeping more than the debt in a tax sale can be a taking .

t: Glossary
x: The idea that a law can be struck down if ordinary people cannot tell what it bans, or if it gives officials too much room to decide who breaks it .

t: The three layers of law
x: Every rule in Williams sits under two other layers of law. When you read a city rule, you are also asking: does it fit the layers above it? Diagram: three layers, highest first. A lower layer must fit inside the ones above it. 1. Federal U.S. Constitution and Bill of Rights; federal laws 2. State California Constitution; state statutes (codes) 3. City Williams Municipal Code (council ordinances) When they clash, the higher layer usually wins.

t: The three layers of law
x: The U.S. Constitution says that it, and federal laws made under it, are "the supreme Law of the Land," and that state judges are bound by them, "any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding" (Article VI) . This is the Supremacy Clause . Read Article VI . The Fourteenth Amendment says "No State shall make or enforce any law" that abridges the privileges or immunities of citizens, and no state shall deprive any person of life, liberty, or property "without due process of law," or deny anyone "the equal protection of the laws" . Read the Fourteenth Amendment . Courts have held that most of the Bill of Rights (such as free speech and protection from unreasonable searches) also limits state and local governments through the Fourteenth Amendment, and that a city is bound the same way the state is .

t: The three layers of law
x: The California Constitution has its own list of rights in Article I, for example free speech (§2), the right to assemble and petition and to see public meetings and records (§3), due process and equal protection (§7), and protection from unreasonable searches (§13) . Read Article I . Article XI, §7 sets the basic rule for cities: "A county or city may make and enforce within its limits all local, police, sanitary, and other ordinances and regulations not in conflict with general laws" . Read Article XI, §7 . State statutes are organized into codes, such as the Government Code and the Elections Code. The official place to read them is leginfo.legislature.ca.gov .

t: The three layers of law
x: Williams is a general law city . In plain terms, its power to make rules comes from state law, and its ordinances may not conflict with the state's general laws . The Williams Municipal Code (WMC) is the city's collection of ordinances passed by the City Council . The official version is on Municode ; a third-party copy on GoCodebook is easier to search but is not official . The layers point to each other. For example, the code's City Council chapter (ch. 2.04) refers readers to state law: "For statutory provisions on city council meetings, see Gov. Code §§ 36801—36815 and §§ 54950—54961" (third-party copy) .

t: The three layers of law
s: Preemption: when a city rule loses
x: Preemption means a higher law pushes aside a lower one. California courts have described three ways a local rule can conflict with state law : It duplicates state law (it repeats what the state already covers). It contradicts state law (it requires what state law bans, or bans what state law requires). It enters a field the state fully occupies (the state has covered the subject so completely that there is no room for local rules). This is called field preemption . Whether a specific Williams rule is preempted is a question for a court, not for this site. The Method helps you gather the facts and questions you would need.

t: The three layers of law
x: Open each question to see the answer. These are general patterns, not answers about any real Williams rule. 1. A state law conflicts with the U.S. Constitution. Which wins? The U.S. Constitution. Article VI makes it "the supreme Law of the Land," binding state judges even if a state's own constitution or laws say otherwise . 2. A Williams ordinance clearly conflicts with a general state law. Which wins? Usually the state law. Article XI, §7 lets a city make ordinances only if they are "not in conflict with general laws" . Courts treat a conflicting local rule as void . The hard part is usually deciding whether there is a conflict. 3. State law says nothing about a subject. Can Williams make a rule about it? Often yes, but check. Article XI, §7 gives cities general power to make local rules . You would still check whether the state has occupied the field, and whether the rule respects constitutional rights such as free speech and due process . 4. A city rule is stricter than a state law on the same subject. Is it allowed? It depends. A court would ask whether the city rule duplicates or contradicts state law, or enters a field the state fully occupies, and whether the state law itself says what cities may do . Read the state statute closely (Method step 3). Go deeper: Constitutions explains both constitutions right by right and sets them next to real Williams code sections. Next

x: General public comment comes near the start of the agenda (item D on the October 21, 2026 agenda). It is for items not listed as public hearings. To speak on an item that is on the agenda, wait until that item comes up . The agenda asks speakers to use the podium and give their name, whether they live in Williams, and any organization they represent. The mayor may set a time limit depending on how many people want to speak . State law: the council must give the public a chance to speak on matters within its jurisdiction. It may set reasonable time limits but may not prohibit criticism of the city's policies or actions. Speakers who use a translator get twice the time (Gov. Code §54954.3) . Courts have upheld shorter time limits . The council generally cannot act on something that is not on the agenda, so a comment can raise an issue but usually can't get a vote that night . Tips: read the packet a few days ahead; write down the item number; bring a short written copy of your comment for the city clerk so it is in the record.

x: If the council takes an action in a way that breaks certain open-meeting rules, you can ask it to undo the action (Gov. Code §54960.1) : Send a written demand to the council describing the action and the violation. Deadline: 90 days after the action, or 30 days if the problem is that the action was not on a properly posted agenda for a meeting held in open session. The council has 30 days to cure or refuse. Silence counts as refusal. You then have 15 days to file in court. There are exceptions (for example, substantial compliance, some contracts relied on in good faith, and tax and debt actions) . x: Under the California Public Records Act , you can ask for city records. The city must tell you within 10 days whether it has disclosable records, and can extend that by up to 14 days in unusual circumstances. The 10 days is to decide , not necessarily to hand everything over . If records are wrongly withheld, you can go to court, and a winning requester can recover attorney's fees . Where to send a request: the city clerk, 810 E Street, Williams, (530) 235-3274 . Describe the records as clearly as you can, keep a copy, and note the date you sent it. t: Who decides?
s: Where the Williams code gives officials a choice over you
x: Most people think a city code is a list of rules. Read the Williams code closely and it's really a list of choices, and residents don't get to make them. One official decides whether you get a ticket or a criminal charge. One decides whether you get a warning or a fine, or both. Another decides whether you're poor enough to argue without paying first. In most of these places the code gives that official no written standard at all. Below are the clauses that matter most, with the exact words, who holds the power, what it means for you, and what a fair version would say. How to read this page. Quotes come from a third-party copy of the code on GoCodebook, in its 2026-10 edition (updated October 3, 2026), re-read October 23, 2026 . The official code is on Municode . Check a quote there or with the city clerk before you rely on it. Lines marked Our reading: are our own reasoning, not a quote. The code shows what officials are allowed to do. Whether they use that power evenly is a question for public records, so ask for them .

s: 1. The city attorney picks: ticket or crime (§1.12.010)
x: "every act prohibited, declared unlawful or declared substandard or unsafe and every failure to perform an act made mandatory by this Code or any other ordinance of the City of Williams shall constitute either a misdemeanor or an infraction, at the discretion of the city attorney." Who holds the power: the city attorney. Williams doesn't employ one. The job is contracted to a private firm, Best Best & Krieger, and partner Andreas Booher serves as city attorney . What it means for you: the same violation can be a misdemeanor, "punishable by a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars or by imprisonment not exceeding six months, or by both" (§1.12.020), or an infraction of $100, $200, then $500 (§1.12.030) . The code lists no factors for that choice, and you get no say in it. It decides more than the fine. Under state law, "An infraction is not punishable by imprisonment," and a person charged with one gets no jury trial and, in most cases, no appointed lawyer . What state law says: "Violation of a city ordinance is a misdemeanor unless by ordinance it is made an infraction" . Our reading: state law lets the council make that call in an ordinance. Williams handed it to the city attorney, case by case. The formula is common in California codes. That makes it widespread, not fair. t: Who decides?
s: 2. Every day is a new offense (§1.12.040)
x: "Each person shall be guilty of a separate offense for each and every day during any portion of which any violation of any provision of the ordinances of the City of Williams is committed, continued or permitted by any such person" Who holds the power: whoever charges or fines you. The rule covers the whole code. What it means for you: a condition that sits for a month can be counted as 30 separate offenses, and nothing in this section requires a notice before the count starts. As infractions, 30 days could add up to $14,300 on paper ($100 + $200 + 28 × $500) . Our reading: courts rarely go near that. The point is the leverage it gives the city in any negotiation. A fair version would say: days count only after written notice and a deadline to fix it, with a cap per condition.

t: Who decides?
x: "'nuisance' and/or 'nuisance condition' means any condition or use of premises or property which is either: (i) detrimental to the premises or property of others; (ii) which poses an immediate or potential health, safety or fire hazard; or (iii) which violates any provision of this Code or other codes adopted by the city." The list that follows includes "Making or emitting any noise uncomfortable to or annoying to a reasonable person," "any condition or use which poses a threat to the public health or safety," trash cans visible "at times other than the day of collection," and buildings that become "a harbor for vagrants, criminals or immoral persons" . Separately, any code violation "shall be deemed to be a public nuisance" (§1.12.050) . Who holds the power: the "enforcement officer," meaning "either the building official, neighborhood services manager, public works director, fire chief, or police chief of the city, or their designees" (§8.16.030(H)) . What it means for you: item (iii) turns every violation, however small, into a nuisance. That unlocks the heavy tools: orders to abate, city cleanup billed to you, liens. Words like "potential" hazard and "immoral persons" give you little way to know in advance what crosses the line. Our reading: vague words don't limit an inspector. They widen what an inspector can pick. A fair version would say: measurable standards (decibel l

t: Who decides?
s: 4. The inspector chooses whether to act, and how hard (§8.16.070, §8.16.110)
x: "In the discretion of the enforcement officer, the administrative citation procedure of Article VI of this chapter may be used either in addition to, or in lieu of, the other provisions of this chapter." (§8.16.070) "he or she may, or upon the direction of the city council shall, serve a notice to abate" (§8.16.110(A)) Who holds the power: the enforcement officer. What it means for you: the officer decides whether to act at all, and then whether to fine you, clean up and bill you, or do both. Two neighbors with the same yard can get two different outcomes, and the code gives no rule for choosing. Our reading: this is the opening for selective enforcement. Nothing here requires the city to log who complained or why one property was picked. What the code already gives you: a citation carries a correction date, and "If a non-emergency health or safety violation(s) is corrected before the correction date provided on the administrative citation, no fine shall be imposed" (§8.16.500(A)) . That protects only that kind of violation, and only on the citation track. It doesn't stop abatement costs, daily counts or a criminal charge. A fair version would say: a written warning and a reasonable window to fix any non-emergency condition before any fine, cost or charge, a published enforcement-priority policy, and public numbers on inspections and citations.

t: Who decides?
s: 5. Entry and water shutoff with no mention of a warrant (§13.04.310, §13.08.060, §13.04.220(E))
x: "have the right of entering any or all premises for the purpose of determining whether the provisions of this chapter are being complied with." (§13.04.310, water) "shall be permitted to enter all properties from which wastes or wastewaters are being or are capable of being discharged into the sewage system" (§13.08.060, sewer) "If any water user refuses entry by, or hinders or prevents inspection by the director or his representative, then the city may discontinue water service to the premises until and unless entry is allowed." (§13.04.220(E)) Who holds the power: the superintendent of streets, "the city" for sewers, and the public works director. What it means for you: read alone, these sections sound like you can't say no, and one of them attaches a price to saying no: your water. None of them mentions a warrant or your consent. What state law says: an inspection warrant is "signed by a judge of a court of record" . The application must include "a statement that consent to inspect has been sought and refused or facts or circumstances reasonably justifying the failure to seek such consent" . A warrant inspection "shall not be made by means of forcible entry" unless the judge expressly allows it, and where consent was refused, notice of the warrant "must be given at least 24 hours before the warrant is executed," unless the judge finds that immediate execution is needed . t: Who decides?
x: "together with either an advance deposit of the fine or an approved request for a deposit waiver." (§8.16.510(A)) "demonstrating to the satisfaction of the city finance officer, or his or her designee, the person's actual financial inability to deposit" … "The written determination of the city finance officer, or his or her designee, shall be final" (§8.16.520(C)–(D)) "Users desiring to dispute an administrative fine shall file a written request for the public works director to reconsider the fine along with full payment of the fine amount within thirty days" (§13.08.930(D), sewer fines up to $5,000 per violation per day) Who holds the power: the finance officer for the hardship waiver; the public works director for sewer fines. What it means for you: to contest a citation, you pay the fine up front or convince a city employee that you can't. That employee's answer is "final." If you can't pay and the city says you can, you lose your hearing before it starts. If you win, the deposit is refunded with interest (§8.16.540(D)) . What state law says: after the city's final decision you can appeal to superior court within 20 days, where the case is heard fresh ("de novo") . A fair version would say: no deposit to ask for a hearing, and any hardship decision can be appealed to the hearing officer.

t: Who decides?
s: 7. The prices aren't in the code (§8.16.490, §13.08.040(E))
x: "as set forth in a schedule of fines established by resolution of the city council." (§8.16.490(A)) "Any other fees the city may deem necessary to carry out this chapter, established from time to time by the city council." (§13.08.040(E)) Who holds the power: the council, usually on a staff recommendation. What it means for you: you can read the entire code and still not know what a violation costs. The amounts sit in separate resolutions, and the sewer chapter leaves room for fees nobody has named yet. Our reading: setting amounts by resolution is legal and common. Not putting them next to the rule is a choice. A fair version would say: every fine schedule and rate resolution printed as an appendix to the code, and "any other fees" deleted.

t: Who decides?
s: 8. The appeal for fines points to a section that doesn't exist (§8.16.590(B))
x: "Such decisions may be appealed pursuant to Section 23.01.692 and Government Code Section 53069.4." Who holds the power: nobody can fix this but the council. What it means for you: the Williams code has no Section 23.01.692 and no Title 23 at all in the copy we checked . Our reading: it was probably copied from another city's code. The state-law appeal (Gov. Code §53069.4) still exists, but a resident following the code's own directions hits a dead end. A fair version would say: the correct section, plus the 20-day court deadline in plain words.

t: Who decides?
s: 9. Costs from the first knock, then a tax sale (§8.16.160, §8.16.180)
x: "the owner and/or responsible party shall also be liable for any expenses and administrative costs incurred by the city, county or any related agency incurred after the initial inspection and identification of the nuisance." (§8.16.160(A)) Those costs can include "costs of investigation" and "the fees and costs of the city's consultants" (§8.16.160(B)), and they "bear interest at the rate of ten percent per annum" (§8.16.160(E)). If they go on the tax roll: "The property may be sold after three years by the tax collector for unpaid delinquent assessments. The tax collector's power of sale shall not be affected by the failure of the property owner to receive notice." (§8.16.180(C)) Who holds the power: the enforcement officer runs up the costs; the council confirms the assessment. What it means for you: the meter starts at the first inspection, including one set off by a neighbor's complaint, and can end with your property sold. What state law says: the tax-sale wording follows state law almost word for word . Our reading: the state picked the tax sale. Williams picked billing from the initial inspection and adding consultant fees. A fair version would say: costs start only after a correction deadline is missed, and no consultant fees without a hearing officer's finding.

t: Who decides?
s: 10. Water bills unpaid 60 days: foreclosure on paper (§13.04.221(E)–(F))
x: "Property subject to a lien for unpaid water charges shall be sold for nonpayment of the same" … "The city attorney is hereby authorized and directed to institute such proceedings, in the name of the city, in any court having jurisdiction over such matters, against any property for which water bill has remained unpaid sixty days after it has been rendered." "The failure of the clerk to record such lien claim or to mail such notice, or the failure of the owner to receive such notice, shall not affect the right to foreclose the lien for unpaid water bills" Who holds the power: the city clerk (lien) and the city attorney (foreclosure). What it means for you: as written, a water bill 60 days overdue is enough to send the city attorney to court against the property, and a notice that never reached you doesn't stop it. Our reading: we have not confirmed the state-law basis for this foreclosure or whether Williams has ever used it. State rules on residential water shutoffs are separate and give more protection. A fair version would say: proof the owner actually got notice, a payment plan offered first, and a council hearing before any foreclosure.

t: Who decides?
x: The law protects you in court. It does much less on your street. Court protection is real. California's anti-SLAPP law lets you ask a court to throw out a lawsuit "arising from any act of that person in furtherance of the person's right of petition or free speech … in connection with a public issue," and a defendant who wins that motion recovers attorney's fees . It does nothing about discretion. No law stops an inspector from suddenly taking an interest in your property, or a permit from slowing down, as long as the official can point to a rule. Our reading: if retaliation comes, it comes through the choices on this page, not through a lawsuit. Habits that protect you (general education, not advice about your case): Know the warrant rules. Outside an emergency, an inspector who doesn't have your consent generally needs a judge's warrant . The warrant application has to say consent was sought and refused, or explain why it wasn't sought . Refusing an inspection "lawfully authorized by warrant" is a misdemeanor, so if there is a warrant, comply and write everything down . At the door it's enough to say: "I don't consent to entry without a warrant. Please leave your card and the code section." Photograph your property before you speak up. Dated photos and video of every side of your home give you a baseline if a "condition" suddenly appears later. Fix the easy things first. Trash

t: Who decides?
s: What to ask the council for
x: The council can change every clause on this page by ordinance. Six asks: Correction first. A written notice and a reasonable window to fix any non-emergency condition before fines or daily counts begin. State law already requires a correction period for continuing building, plumbing, electrical and zoning violations that aren't an immediate danger , and Williams' citation rules waive the fine when a non-emergency health or safety violation is fixed by the correction date (§8.16.500(A)) . Extend that to every non-emergency violation and every enforcement track: citations, abatement costs and criminal charges. Criteria for misdemeanor vs. infraction. Write the factors into §1.12.010, require written reasons, and publish yearly counts. Fix the dead cross-reference in §8.16.590(B) and the other wrong section numbers. Put the fine schedule in the code, and delete "Any other fees the city may deem necessary." Warrant language in every entry clause. Copy §8.08.090's own words, "after obtaining either a warrant or permission," into the water and sewer chapters, and drop water shutoff for refusing an inspection. No deposit to contest a fine, and an appeal from the finance officer's hardship decision. Bring these to public comment or put them in a letter to the council. Quote the section number every time.
